characteristics.cultivar: Camellia sinensis var. assamica, ancient arbor trees aged 200–300+ years

description.short: One of the most expensive and exquisite sheng pu-erh terroirs — exceptional sweetness with almost no bitterness
description.overview: Bingdao village in the Mengku mountains rivals Lao Banzhang for the crown of elite pu-erh terroirs, but takes an entirely different path — not through brute power, but through supreme purity, rock-sugar sweetness, and a soothing cooling sensation.
description.leaf: Large, thick dark-green leaves from ancient arbor trees
description.aroma: Exquisite honeyed, floral bouquet with notes of rock sugar and fresh mountain air
description.taste: Exceptionally sweet from the very first infusion, virtually devoid of bitterness and harsh astringency, boasting a silken, nectar-like texture
description.aftertaste: Extraordinarily long and sweet, leaving a lingering cool, refreshing sensation in the throat (reminiscent of its name, "ice island")
description.processing: Hand-harvesting from old trees → withering → gentle low-temperature fixation → rolling → sun-drying → steam compression into cakes

history.origin: The name Bingdao translates literally to "Ice Island" (a phonetic rendering from the indigenous Dai language, also evocative of the tea's refreshing cool sensation in the throat)
history.development: Much like Lao Banzhang, world-class fame arrived relatively recently — during the 2000s and 2010s — when connoisseurs specifically sought out the unmistakable rock-candy sweetness of its ancient arbor trees
history.modern: Today authentic raw material from old Bingdao trees ranks among the most expensive tea leaves in the world, making it a frequent target for counterfeiting
interestingFacts: Bingdao and Lao Banzhang are often compared as the two royal poles of luxury pu-erh: Lao Banzhang represents strength and majesty (the King), while Bingdao represents grace, sweetness, and delicacy (the Queen)
Because authentic Bingdao old-tree leaves fetch astronomical prices, much of the tea labeled "Bingdao" on the market originates from surrounding, lower-altitude areas of Mengku
